title: Conduct a range of livestock husbandry practices in extensive farming conditions

lessons.title: Grazing, water and lick in the veld
lessons.html:
Grazing, water and lick in the veld

In this work experience module you take part in the husbandry work of an extensive farm: moving animals between camps, keeping water and lick available, breeding work, births, weaning, marking and handling. You record each task in a logbook signed by your supervisor.

Following the grazing plan

The farm's grazing plan shows which camp each herd or flock should be in and when it moves. Before moving animals:

  • Check that the new camp has water, lick, sound fences and closed gates to other camps.
  • Check for poisonous plants, especially after fire or early rain.
  • Move animals quietly in the cool part of the day, at the pace of the slowest animals.
  • Count animals out of the old camp and into the new one.
  • Record the date and numbers on the grazing record.

Observing the veld

Learn to judge grass cover and recovery. Note when the best grasses are being grazed short, when bare patches or erosion appear, and when bush is encroaching. Report this to the supervisor so the grazing plan can be adjusted. Do not let animals return to a camp before it has rested as planned.

Water infrastructure

Extensive farms depend on boreholes, windmills, solar pumps, pipelines, reservoirs and troughs. On every round:

  • Check that water is flowing and troughs are full and clean.
  • Check for leaks in pipes and reservoirs.
  • Check float valves and windmill or pump operation.
  • Report problems urgently - in hot weather animals cannot go long without water.

Lick management

Put out the correct seasonal lick in covered troughs. Estimate intake by recording bags put out and number of animals. Report intake far above or below the supplier's guideline so the supervisor can adjust the mix or placement.

lessons.title: Breeding, birth and weaning on the veld
lessons.html:
Breeding, birth and weaning on the veld

The breeding season

Help to prepare bulls and rams: check their feet, legs, condition and testes, and confirm they have had their breeding soundness evaluation. Put them with the females on the planned date and in the right numbers for the camp. Watch that males are working and not injured. Remove them on the planned date to keep the birth season short.

Pregnancy and birth

After pregnancy diagnosis, pregnant females may be managed as a separate group. Before the birth season, move them to camps with good grazing, shelter, and easy access for checking. During the season:

  • Check the group at least morning and evening.
  • Watch for females in difficulty and call the supervisor.
  • Check that each newborn suckles and has a full belly.
  • Tag or mark young and record dam, date and sex.
  • Look after orphans and weak young as the farm instructs.

Protecting young stock

Lambs and kids are most at risk of predators and cold in the first days. Use the farm's methods: night kraals, lambing camps near the homestead, guard animals or shepherding. Record losses and causes.

Weaning

Weaning is usually done at a fixed age or weight, before winter sets in, so mothers can regain condition. On weaning day:

  1. Gather calmly and separate mothers and young.
  2. Weigh the young and record weights against the dam's number.
  3. Do routine treatments due at weaning according to the health plan.
  4. Move weaners to a good camp with clean water, lick or creep feed.
  5. Watch them closely for the next few days.

Weaning weights help the farm select the best mothers and replacement heifers or ewes.

lessons.title: Handling, marking and selecting stock
lessons.html:
Handling, marking and selecting stock

Handling extensive animals

Veld animals are less tame, so calm handling is vital for safety and production. Work at the edge of the flight zone, move slowly, keep groups together and avoid shouting, whips and dogs in confined spaces. Stand clear of gates when animals are moving through. Always have an escape route in the kraal. Bulls, cows with calves and rams must be treated with caution.

Identification

Tag, tattoo or brand animals as the farm requires and record numbers in the register. Brand marks used for ownership must be registered and placed correctly. Clean ear tag applicators between animals and tag in the correct part of the ear.

Routine procedures

Castration, tail docking, dehorning and hoof care are done at the correct age and by the method the farm and vet set, with pain relief where required. Take part under supervision and only do procedures alone once you are signed off as competent.

Body condition scoring

Practise scoring condition by feeling the backbone, ribs and tail head. Score breeding females at key times: before breeding, mid-pregnancy, birth and weaning. Low scores before breeding mean fewer pregnancies; tell the supervisor.

Selection and culling

KeepCull
Females that wean a good young every yearFemales that skip years or lose young repeatedly
Sound udders, feet, legs and teethBroken mouths, bad udders, chronic lameness
Calm temperamentAggressive or wild animals

Logbook and reflection

Record every husbandry task with date, animals, your role and signature. Reflect weekly on what you learned and what to practise.

Key points

  • Check water, lick, fences and plants before moving animals to a new camp.
  • Count animals out and in on every move.
  • Keep the birth season short and check pregnant groups morning and evening.
  • Weigh at weaning to support selection.
  • Handle veld animals calmly with an escape route ready.
